title: Mysterious Asteroid's Acceleration is Defying Expectations as Scientists Anticipate New Clues from a 2031 Spacecraft Encounter
excerpt: New research is challenging presumptions about a suspected "dark comet" exhibiting unusual acceleration in its orbit around the Sun.
content:
New questions have emerged over the identity of a space object displaying odd acceleration, which calls into question whether it may fall within an elusive class of objects astronomers call “dark comets.”

The object, dubbed 1998 KY26, measures just 36 feet across and rotates every five and a half minutes. Presently characterized as an asteroid, the small object has baffled astronomers because of the subtle, but unusual acceleration it exhibits while orbiting the Sun.

One potential explanation for this could be water vapor that escapes from the asteroid as the Sun heats its exterior, which would be capable of producing propulsion like that of a comet, but without the visible “coma” or tail astronomers expect to see on such objects.

However, newly published research is challenging that interpretation of what could be causing the object’s unusual behavior, ahead of a 2031 spacecraft encounter that may finally grant astronomers a chance at solving the mystery.

Pouring Water on an Icy Asteroid Theory

In a recent study, researchers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi at the Georgia Institute of Technology used three-dimensional computer simulations to determine whether an asteroid would be capable of possessing enough ice to cause the non-gravitational acceleration 1998 KY26 currently displays.

Based on the team’s findings, they now believe that temperatures throughout the suspected space rock are likely to be too warm for any water ice to be maintained over extended periods.

“Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid’s composition,” the researchers write in their study.

Even if as little as one percent of 1998 KY26’s mass was attributed to water, Hansen and Hirabayashi say their calculations reveal the asteroid would still lose its ice within around 2,000 years.

So what might be causing the asteroid’s odd non-gravitational acceleration?

Heat Radiation as an Alternative

One idea Hansen and Hirabayashi put forward in their study is that pressure from sunlight and thermal radiation offers a better potential explanation for what astronomers are currently observing.

Fortunately, determining the exact identity of 1998 KY26 may be possible in the coming years. Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft will reach 1998 KY26 sometime in 2031, potentially allowing astronomers a much clearer look at the unusual asteroid and possibly answer the mystery of its acceleration.

The recent paper, “Thermally unfavorable conditions of volatile existence in near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26, the Hayabusa extended mission’s target,” by Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi, appeared in the journal Icarus.
